# Balance of power (`balance_of_power`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by international_law_sovereignty, deterrence, security_dilemma_arms_race, military_intelligence_codebreaking
- Core idea: In a system of several independent states, each is safest when none is strong enough to dominate the rest. So states should combine against whichever is becoming strongest, whatever its religion or past friendship, and should not destroy a beaten rival who may be needed as a counterweight tomorrow. Resident ambassadors helped Italian rulers track shifts in strength. Earlier states also balanced rivals through envoys and shifting alliances. Its aim is the independence of the members, not peace: it works through the threat of war and through limited wars.
- Pitfalls:
  - It preserves the great powers, not peace or the small states (Poland was partitioned in its name, 1772–1795)
  - Each waits for another to bear the cost of resisting (buck-passing), or all are dragged in by one ally (1914)
  - It breaks down when the members invite an outside power into their quarrels, as Milan invited France into Italy in 1494
  - Power is hard to measure, and miscalculating it causes the wars the system should prevent
  - It can fail completely: in China it ended in conquest by Qin in 221 BC
- History: mesopotamia: 14th c. BC – Amarna letters show a club of great kings (Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni, Babylon, Assyria) managing parity by gifts and marriage; greece: 5th–4th c. BC – Athens, Sparta and Thebes combine in turn against the strongest; c. 150 BC – Polybius I.83 praises Hiero of Syracuse for propping up Carthage against Rome; india: c. 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Arthashastra: circle of states (mandala), where the neighbour is the enemy and the neighbour's neighbour the ally, and six policies from peace to dual policy; china: 4th–3rd c. BC – 'vertical' alliances against Qin and Qin's 'horizontal' counter-alliances; europe: 1454 – Peace of Lodi between Milan and Venice; 1454–55 – Italian League comes to include Milan, Venice, Florence, Naples and the pope; to 1492 – Lorenzo de' Medici as the balancer, in Guicciardini's account; 1494 – collapse with the French invasion; 1713 – Treaty of Utrecht names the 'just balance of power'; 1752 – Hume's essay; 1815 – Vienna settlement and Concert of Europe
- Read:
  - Francesco Guicciardini, Storia d'Italia, book I (written 1537–1540, printed 1561)
  - David Hume, Of the Balance of Power (1752)
  - Garrett Mattingly, Renaissance Diplomacy (1955)
